Need to search first.I've written notes for verses 1–4, 5–18, 19–24 and 25–28 below. They rest mostly on older Protestant commentaries and David Guzik's Enduring Word. I couldn't find any page where Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed, Lutheran or Anglican teachers disagree over these verses, so that section is mostly a gap. The other-views section is also thin, because my search tool stopped working before I could look at bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org's own notes, newadvent.org's Bible commentary, catholic.com or oca.org.

Two caveats about the sources:
- **Search snippets:** most of the full page downloads failed, so many notes are based on the long snippets the search tool returned rather than whole pages.
- **Unlabelled comments:** several comments on the Biblehub verse pages had no commentator's name attached. I've called them "unnamed" rather than guess who wrote them.

---

## 1. The traditional reading

**vv. 1–2 (the journeys, written down at God's command)**
- Guzik says the chapter records 42 places, from Rameses to the plains of Moab. Before crossing the Jordan, the second generation needed to remember God's faithfulness over 40 years, and remembering past goodness prepared them for the conquest ahead. He quotes Ronald Allen: most sites were desert camps that left no archaeological trace, so they are hard to map. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/
- Matthew Henry says God had Moses keep a journal of notable events on the way, both for his own reflection and to teach others. On v. 1, he says Israel left "with their armies," in ranks like an army, under Moses and Aaron as guides under God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_033.cfm
- Precept Austin collects several writers here:
  - Constable notes that Moses lists the places Israel set out *from*, not where they stopped, which keeps attention on the goal: the Promised Land.
  - Sprinkle calls Moses' record a kind of journaling. He says Scripture doesn't command it but it is a good practice for believers.
  - John Currid says the list reminds Israel that God cared for them even in a barren wasteland, and that they got this far only by God's grace.
  - Wiersbe stresses that God plans history and carries out his plan.
  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-33-commentary
- Keil & Delitzsch (Hebrew detail): the march is described by the places they set out from, which is why "and they broke up" keeps repeating. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-9.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the phrase "by the commandment of the LORD" can be read as describing the marches themselves, meaning God ordered each move. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/33.htm
- The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (unabridged) commentary gives three reasons for keeping the record: to confirm the history is true, to preserve a memorial of God's acts for Israel, and to strengthen their faith before invading Canaan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/numbers-33.html

**v. 3 (marching out "defiantly," literally "with a high hand")**
- Guzik: after centuries of slavery, God let them leave boldly, as conquerors rather than runaway slaves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/
- Allen (via Precept Austin): in Numbers 15:30 the same Hebrew phrase means open defiance of God. Here it is positive, a picture of triumph under the Lord's higher hand of blessing. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-33-commentary
- Matthew Henry: their hand was "high" because God's hand was working for them. They didn't slip away in secret (he cites Isaiah 52:12). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_033.cfm
- Gill (on Biblehub): they left openly and boldly, and the Egyptians were powerless to stop them, even glad to see them go. The Pulpit Commentary adds that the departure began at night (Exodus 12:42) and carried on into the next day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-3.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary calls the departure both public (nothing secret or shameful about it) and triumphant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-33.html

**v. 4 (the Egyptians burying their firstborn; judgment on their gods)**
- Gill:
  - Grief and burials kept the Egyptians too busy to bother Israel, and they knew the blow had come because they kept Israel captive.
  - He says Egypt's idols were shaken and broken, linking this to Isaiah 19:1.
  - He reports the Targum of Jonathan's claim that Egypt's idols melted, crumbled or turned to ash.
  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-33.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-4.htm
- Matthew Henry thinks the idols were probably broken down, as Dagon later fell before the ark, so the Egyptians couldn't consult them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/33-4.html
- Guzik says the plagues were deliberately aimed at Egypt's gods, to humble people who believed in them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/
- Other readings of "their gods" on the Biblehub commentary page (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-4.htm):
  - **Poole** gives two options. "Gods" may mean Egypt's princes and rulers, so that even the king's firstborn died. Or it may mean the sacred animals, which died along with the firstborn of beasts.
  - **Geneva Study Bible:** either the idols or the men in authority.
  - **An unnamed commentator** gives the same two options: rulers or idols.
  - **A second unnamed commentator** says false gods exist only in people's minds, so they could only be "judged" by being made contemptible in the eyes of those who feared them.

**vv. 5–10 (Rameses to the Red Sea camp)**
- Guzik treats vv. 5–10 as the first of six groups of seven stops (compare Exodus 12–16). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/
- Keil & Delitzsch: the stops from Succoth to Sinai match Exodus, except that Exodus leaves out the Red Sea camp (v. 10) and Dophkah and Alush. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-3.htm
- Matthew Henry:
  - At first they camped on the "edge" of the wilderness (v. 6) and later deep inside it, as God prepares his people for bigger trials with smaller ones.
  - "Our removals in this world are but from one wilderness to another."
  - They were led back and forth as if through a maze, yet always under the pillar of cloud and fire.
  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_033.cfm
- v. 7 (turning back to Pi-hahiroth): the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary has sermon outlines titled "Standing still in the midst of danger" and "Going forward in the face of difficulties." It also says the route, though contrary to Israel's hopes, was the safest path to Canaan, so we should leave the choice of our way to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-33.html
- v. 8: an unnamed commentator on Biblehub says the missing "pi" in "Hahiroth" is just a common Egyptian prefix, and that the "wilderness of Etham" is the part of the wilderness of Shur next to Etham. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-12.htm
- v. 9 (Elim):
  - Guzik and F. B. Meyer both point out that the list passes over Israel's grumbling at Marah but lingers on Elim's springs and palms. Guzik's page presents this as a picture of God forgetting forgiven sins; Meyer says the memory of the seventy palms survived years of hard travel, and encourages readers to remember God's past kindnesses.
  - Gill says Elim was eight miles from Marah and was chosen for its water.
  - JFB identifies it with Wadi Ghurundel.
  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/, https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-33-commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-9.htm
- v. 9, symbolic readings (Biblehub's own study notes, not a named commentator): the twelve springs stand for the twelve tribes, each provided for, and the seventy palms for the seventy elders or the seventy nations of Genesis 10. https://biblehub.com/study/numbers/33-9.htm and https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_12_springs_70_palms.htm
- v. 10 (the Red Sea camp): Adam Clarke admits the spot is hard to place, since they were already heading east toward Sinai. He suggests it is called "by the Red Sea" because the sea was still the main thing in view, and notes this stop appears nowhere else. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/numbers/33.htm

**vv. 11–14 (Desert of Sin, Dophkah, Alush, Rephidim)**
- Clarke: the Desert of Sin lies between Elim and Sinai. Dophkah and Alush are not in Exodus and their locations are unknown. Rephidim is remembered for the rebellion over water (Exodus 17). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/numbers/33.htm
- Gill: Dophkah came after the manna was given. He records Jewish tradition that the Targum calls Alush "the strong fort" and that Israel kept its first Sabbath there (Exodus 16:30). On v. 14 he retells the striking of the rock. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-33.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-13.htm
- An unnamed commentator on Biblehub says Exodus leaves out Dophkah and Alush, apparently because nothing remarkable happened there. JFB places the three stops in the valleys of El Sheikh and Feiran, about four days' march for so large a crowd. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-12.htm
- Guzik: even unknown places like Dophkah and Alush matter as places where the Lord's army marched toward the promised land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/

**vv. 15–17 (Sinai, Kibroth-hattaavah, Hazeroth)**
- Guzik quotes a comparison: Numbers 10–13 names only three stops between Sinai and Kadesh, while vv. 16–36 list twenty-two. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary notes Hazeroth as the place where Miriam and Aaron rebelled against Moses. Whedon suggests it is the site Hudhera, citing Ridgaway. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-33.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-33.html

**v. 18 (Rithmah)**
- Barnes: the name comes from *retem*, the broom plant (the KJV's "juniper"). He says this must be the same camp Numbers 13:26 places at Kadesh, where the spies were sent from. Poole likewise puts it near Kadesh-barnea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-18.htm
- Gill reports that some scholars equate it with Kadesh-barnea. He also mentions Rashi's idea that the name recalls the spies' "evil tongue," linked to Psalm 120:3–4 and its "coals of juniper." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-18.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch argue the same identification at length and connect the name with Wadi Abu Retemat, south of Kadesh. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html
- Whedon says the site has not been identified. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-33.html

**vv. 19–24 (Rimmon-perez to Haradah)**
- Guzik's third group of seven. He lists suggested name meanings from Allen, Clarke and Trapp: Rithmah "binding," Rimmon-perez "pomegranate breach," Libnah "white," Rissah unknown, Kehelathah "assembly," Mount Shepher "mount of beauty," Haradah "frightening." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/
- Barnes: from v. 19 onward the stops belong to the years of punishment wandering. He suggests Korah's rebellion may have happened at Rimmon-perez. An unnamed commentator notes that the Targum instead links that rebellion to Kehelathah ("assembly"). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-19.htm
- JFB (unabridged): 18 stops lie between Hazeroth and Kadesh, but that trip took only eleven days (Deuteronomy 1:2). So these stops must belong to the roughly 38 years between Israel's two visits to Kadesh. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/numbers-33.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: the names in vv. 19–30 are camps from the 37 years of punishment, on Israel's slow move back from Kadesh toward the Red Sea. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html
- Whedon says scholars broadly agree on this, and quotes the observation that the camps were chosen near water and vegetation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-33.html
- An unnamed commentator on Biblehub: there was no fixed line of march in this period. Israel probably stayed within the wilderness of Paran, apart from trips along the Arabah valley. Rissah, Haradah and Tahath may match Rasa, Aradeh and Elthi on Roman road maps. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-24.htm
- Gill gives distances: about six miles between stops, then four. https://www.studylight.org/bible/pol/ubg/numbers/33-26.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary gives identifications quoted from the Speaker's Commentary, such as Mount Shepher as Jebel-esh-Shureif. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-33.html

**vv. 25–28 (Makheloth, Tahath, Terah, Mithkah)**
- Guzik's fourth group, which runs Makheloth to Bene-jaakan (compare Deuteronomy 10). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/
- The ISBE dictionary on net.bible.org gives these meanings: Makheloth "gatherings," Tahath probably "below" (the descent into the Arabah), Terah "delay" (rest in better pasture), Mithkah "sweetness" of pasture or water. It adds that most sites on this stretch are unknown. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Wanderings+Of+Israel

**Whole passage: devotional themes**
- Matthew Henry: "God led them about, yet led them the right way." Believers should likewise remember God's care for them, their families and their land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-18.htm
- Jensen (via Precept Austin): the chapter shows God's patient grace in keeping his people through all these places. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-33-commentary
- Allen (via Precept Austin): the list mentions no rebellion, only steady progress. The new generation is treated as if it were the one that left Egypt. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-33-commentary

## 2. Differences between Protestant traditions
I found no page showing these traditions disagreeing over vv. 1–28. The readings above are broadly the same across Gill, Henry, Clarke, the Pulpit Commentary and Guzik. (StudyLight tags Gill as "Baptist · Calvinism" at https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/33-9.html.)

The nearest thing to a distinctive emphasis is Adam Clarke's comments on the chapter. He sees Israel's unsettled wandering as a picture of unsettled religion under the law (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/numbers-33.html). He also warns against believers settling into the belief that sin must live in them for as long as they live (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/numbers/33.htm). I couldn't find a page that sets this against another tradition's view, so I'm only reporting what he says.

## 3. Other views
- **Church Father (Jerome):** in Letter 78 to Fabiola, Jerome wrote a treatise on the 42 "mansions," or stopping places. CCEL's summary says he makes them a picture of the Christian's pilgrimage from earth to heaven. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf206.v.LXXVIII.html. In Letter 77 he mentions he was working on this at Fabiola's request when she died, and pictures her as having crossed the world's wilderness into the promised land. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3001077.htm
- **Critical questions:**
  - Allen (via Precept Austin) takes the list as accurate. But he thinks the forty sites, one for each year, show some deliberate arrangement and may have been a memory aid, which would explain why some places are left in or out. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-33-commentary
  - The Pulpit Commentary says that whether v. 2 supports Moses writing the rest of Numbers is a separate question, which it handles in its Introduction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/33.htm
- **A debated numbering theory:** Coffman argues the exact count of 42 stops is the main point of the chapter. He sees it behind the "forty-two months" of Revelation, which he takes to stand for the church's present era. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/33-42.html
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of these verses.
